I.1.title: Learning, friends, and not being known
I.1.reflection: The book opens with three questions, each answered by itself. Learning is a pleasure when it is practised over time, friends who come from far away are a joy, and the last line turns inward: the measure of a person is how they bear being overlooked. The order runs from the self, to company, to the world's indifference.
I.1.question: Which of the three is hardest for you today: to keep at something, to welcome someone, or to go unnoticed without resentment?

I.2.title: The root
I.2.reflection: Master Yu, one of the disciples, argues that people who are good to their parents and elder brothers rarely stir up trouble. His image is of a tree: attend to the root, and the branches follow. The household comes first in this order of things, and the larger virtue grows out of it.
I.2.question: What in your own life works as a root, so that other things grow from it without effort?

I.3.title: Fine words
I.3.reflection: One sentence, and it returns more than once in the book. Smooth talk and an ingratiating face are rarely found together with real goodness. It does not say they never are; it says they seldom are, and asks us to notice the pattern.
I.3.question: When were you last persuaded more by how something was said than by what was said?

I.4.title: Three questions a day
I.4.reflection: Master Zeng examines himself each day on three points: whether he was faithful in working for others, sincere with friends, and whether he practised what he was taught. The questions are about conduct, not feelings, and each one names a relation: the people he serves, his friends, his teacher.
I.4.question: If you asked yourself three questions every evening, what would they be?
I.4.exercise: Tonight, before sleep, ask Zeng's three questions of the day just past, and answer each in a single honest sentence.

I.5.title: A state of a thousand chariots
I.5.reflection: Government here is a short list: attention to affairs, good faith, thrift, care for people, and calling on the people's labour only in the right season, when the fields can spare them. A thousand chariots meant a middling state. The advice is practical before it is lofty.
I.5.question: Which item on this list would matter most in a place you know, a workplace or a town?

I.6.title: Study comes after
I.6.reflection: A young person's duties are named in order: be good at home, respectful outside, careful and truthful, kind to all and close to the good. Only when there is strength to spare should they turn to letters. Conduct is the first lesson and books the second.
I.6.question: Do you think conduct can be learned before reading, or only through it?

I.7.title: He has learned, says Zixia
I.7.reflection: Zixia describes someone who prefers worth to beauty, gives their full strength to their parents and their life to their lord, and keeps faith with friends. Even if people say this person never studied, Zixia insists they have. Learning is judged by what it produces.
I.7.question: Whom do you know who never studied in the usual sense and yet has learned, in Zixia's sense?

I.8.title: Faults, and not fearing to change
I.8.reflection: Four short rules: be serious, or learning will not hold; put good faith first; do not befriend those who are not your equals; when you have faults, do not be afraid to correct them. The third rule is often read as "befriend those who can help you grow". The last is the one the book returns to.
I.8.question: What fault have you been slow to correct, and what makes correcting it frightening?

I.9.title: Remembering the dead
I.9.reflection: Master Zeng ties public virtue to how carefully the dead are mourned and the long departed remembered in sacrifice. Care for those who can no longer repay it is, for him, what makes a people's character deep. The rites are a form of memory.
I.9.question: How do the people around you remember those who came before them?

I.10.title: How the Master learns about a state
I.10.reflection: Ziqin wonders whether Confucius asks for news of each government or is simply told. Zigong answers that the Master is gentle, upright, courteous, frugal and deferential, and so people tell him. His way of asking is not to ask in the usual way at all.
I.10.question: Have you found that people tell you more when you press, or when you are the kind of person they want to tell?

I.11.title: Three years
I.11.reflection: While a father lives, look at the son's intentions; after his death, look at his conduct. If for three years he keeps to his father's way, he may be called filial. The three years match the length of mourning. The chapter returns almost word for word as IV.20.
I.11.question: What would it mean to keep someone's way for a time after they are gone, and when should the keeping end?

I.12.title: Ease within the form
I.12.reflection: Master Yu says that in ritual, harmony and ease are what matter most, and the old kings prized them in great and small things alike. Yet ease that is not held by ritual will not do either. Form without ease is stiff; ease without form drifts.
I.12.question: Where in your day is there a form you keep that also lets you be at ease?

I.13.title: Promises that can be kept
I.13.reflection: When a promise is close to what is right, it can be kept. When respect is close to what is proper, it keeps shame away. When you rely on people who will not let you down, they can be relied on to the end. Each clause is about choosing well at the beginning.
I.13.question: Is there a promise you made that you could keep only because it was right to begin with?

I.14.title: Loving to learn
I.14.reflection: Confucius describes someone who does not seek a full stomach or a comfortable house, is quick in action and careful in speech, and goes to those who have the Way to be set straight. Such a person, he says, loves learning. Learning is again a matter of a whole life, not of books alone.
I.14.question: Who would you go to, today, to be set straight?

I.15.title: Cut, file, carve, polish
I.15.reflection: Zigong is pleased with being poor without flattery and rich without pride. Confucius answers that it is better still to be poor and joyful, rich and fond of ritual. Zigong recognises a line from the Odes about cutting and polishing jade: good is not the end, it can be worked further. The Master is delighted that he made the leap himself.
I.15.question: What in you is good enough already, and could still be polished?

I.16.title: Not knowing others
I.16.reflection: The first book ends where it began, with being unknown. Confucius is not troubled that others do not know him; he is troubled that he does not know them. The worry is turned around and given a task.
I.16.question: Whom have you failed to understand, while worrying that you were not understood?
